runs.text: Reckoning never came kindly. It kicked the door in and dragged us out; no one was left standing.

I was twenty when I walked away from an abusive husband and went back to my mother’s house. By then, her new boyfriend was living there, and the pills hadn’t gone away like she had told me. I knew better, but when she asked me to pick up her prescription, I caved. She cried. She made her pain my problem once again. I wanted to believe the sob story. I wanted to believe in her.

I was arrested for five felony counts of prescription fraud. I told the detectives the truth, told them about my mother, about the pills, about all of it. Sad part is they knew I was telling the truth. I was sentenced to three years in a maximum-security prison. Let me be clear I was an adult I knew what I was doing was wrong. It took me an exceedingly long time to be accountable for this.
That’s how reckoning works. There’s no hero, just a line you’ve crossed and the price you must pay. Sometimes the ones who are supposed to save you are the ones who place you in the fire.
This section is about naming the cost, refusing to apologize for making it out alive, and putting the truth on record, no matter who’s listening.
She doesn’t sing to seduce.
She sings to remember.
Her songs are what grief sounds like
when it finally finds a voice.
It lures men, yes
but only because they can recognize
something in her tune
They’ve never dared to admit.
She doesn’t want your damn ship.
She wants your pain torn free.
She wants your shame confessed and released.
She wants you to name what haunts you
before it kills you.
She is not a danger or a threat.
She is the consequence of ignoring your truth
for too long.
She builds her blueprints
with sorrows and intuition.
She’s never once followed a rule
she didn’t dismantle first.
Her cathedral isn’t made of stone.
It’s made from a knowing
A knowing that comes
after watching too many homes destroyed and still choosing to build anyway.
She designs with her scar tissue.
Reinforces with boundaries.
She does not decorate.
She fortifies.
If you ever enter her world,
you better know who you truly are
or be ready to find out.
The guards called me Tyson.
Said it at count like a nickname.
I kept leaving bruises on the day.
I did not have words for warning.
Fists did the talking.
Metal bunks. Bright lights. A body on alarm.
I was not evil. I was injured.
Anger wore my face for me.
Pain walked in first and chose the target.
I swung to say back off.
I swung to say I exist.
I swung because help felt smaller than a fist.
Hurt people hurt people.
I was one of them.
Now I fight different.
Fight for breath before the flare.
Fight for quiet, for truth said early.
Hands open when I can.
Only close when I must.
I used to beg for authenticity,
like it was something I could get
by enduring just long enough.
But pain wasn’t proof
and the silence isn’t peace
and obedience never once saved me.
What did save me
was the burn.
The collapse.
The day I got over lying to myself
to keep the story clean for everyone else.
I don’t owe the world a palatable version of me.
Not the soft-spoken, keep it smiling one
who ate her grief and called it growth.
Truth lives where the rupture is.
Where the voice whispers.
Where the heart screams,
Not this again. Not anymore.
So let it burn.
Let the false parts fall away.
Let the people who only knew me when I was invisible
stay confused.
I will not come back smaller
to make anyone more comfortable.
I am building a life that fits the size of my spirit.
Even if no one cares.
Even if no one stays.
Even if I have to walk it alone.
This is the only path.
And I am finally on it.
They handed me a blackboard
and said, draw your future.
So I picked out my chalk
like it was a knife set.
One white.
One red.
One broken in half
but still good enough to mark
what mattered.
I drew a door,
then walked through it.
Drew a fire,
then warmed my hands.
Drew my name
not the one they gave me,
the one I took back
when I stopped hiding in the void.
They thought the chalk was just dust.
But they were wrong: it’s my bones.
It’s memory.
It’s the proof I was here,
I saw it all,
and I still dared to draw something new.
